articles.title: “Sit Nice!”: Peer Culture, Teacher Capacity, and Joint Socialization Efforts in Preschool
articles.abstract: Preschools instill soft skills that are crucial to children’s life outcomes. As preschool access expands, research and policy often focus on improving teacher quality. This focus downplays how much teachers’ efforts may depend on children’s peers. Drawing on two years of ethnography, I highlight two important aspects of socialization: teachers’ capacity to deliver messages in the moment, and peers’ tendency to support those messages. I compare socialization processes at two race- and class-segregated preschools. Three interrelated classroom conditions—children’s enrollment, attendance, and challenging behaviors—mattered for socialization interactions. Teachers at both preschools pursued socialization goals of instilling safe and formal classroom behaviors. At the affluent, majority-White preschool, teachers had a greater capacity to coach children in the moment, and peers had a culture of supporting teacher messages. At the low-income, racially diverse preschool, children placed the authority to coach classroom behavior in their teachers, who were pressed for time. I argue that socialization agents jointly influence behavior. In segregated preschools, teachers may shape classroom behavior to unequal extents, preventing early learning settings from disrupting future inequalities.

Intergenerational Educational Mobility and Subjective Social Status in Japan
articles.abstract: Individuals’ evaluations of their own social positions reflect not only their current socioeconomic standing but also the trajectory that led them there. Although it has been argued that individuals’ subjective social status (SSS) is shaped by intergenerational mobility experiences, empirical investigation remains limited. The authors examine how intergenerational educational mobility relates to SSS using the diagonal reference model applied to data from multiple nationally representative surveys in Japan. The results indicate that educational origin remains significantly associated with SSS even net of destination and that downward educational mobility is negatively associated with SSS, with the strength of the association intensifying with mobility distance. These associations hold comparably for both men and women. These results are largely robust to different operationalizations of parental educational attainment, after controlling for other socioeconomic characteristics or separating cohorts. These findings suggest that not only current status but also origin and mobility trajectories jointly shape individuals’ SSS. Moreover, the results imply that downward educational mobility is particularly associated with individuals’ lower evaluation of their own social positions in Japan, where educational credentials retain high symbolic value despite educational expansion.
